newsitem.title: CANADA: Bre-X defends Busang claim, stock wreaks havoc in Toronto.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X defends Busang claim, stock wreaks havoc in Toronto.

text.p: Bre-X Minerals Ltd. on Thursday defended its claim to have found the richest gold strike in the world, but the Canadian gold company failed to calm panicky investors who lopped more than C$3 billion ($2.2 billion) off its stock market value.

Barely 24 hours after admitting the Busang deposit in Indonesia may be nowhere near as rich as projected, Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh declared he was confident of the company's reserve estimates for the site deep in the jungles of Indonesia's Borneo island.

"We remain and have every confidence that there is the reserve potential in the Busang property that we have stated," Walsh told reporters at an impromptu news conference outside Bre-X's Calgary, Alberta, headquarters.

While Canadian securities regulators scrambled to investigate the biggest mining controversy in decades, Indonesia said it was withholding the company's applications for crucial contracts of work to develop the property.

Huge questions still loom over Bre-X's claim to have found the world's biggest gold field while its operating partner, Freeport McMoran Copper & Gold, an experienced U.S. mining concern, has cautioned its own studies turned up only "insignificant amounts of gold.".
"All of these questions are unanswered and, therefore, the Street is operating in a vacuum," said John Ing, president of the Maison Placements Canada Inc. brokerage in Toronto.
Walsh asserted it was "physically impossible" to tamper with core samples from the deposit and added that he stood behind Bre-X's technical work at Busang.

It was all too much for jittery Bre-X shareholders who drove the stock down C$12.55 ($9.09) to C$2.95 ($2.13) in massive turnover of 6.7 million shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange when the stock resumed trading late in Thursday's session.
The stock had been halted since Tuesday's close.
Bre-X, which soared to C$250 ($181) from mere pennies before a 10-for-1 stock split, last traded at C$15.50 ($11.23) before it was halted on Wednesday.

The dramatic sell-off dragged Canada's biggest stock market down by 191.2 points, or 3.12 percent, and prompted investors to dump other small mining stocks. It was the biggest fall on the Toronto Stock Exchange since Oct. 20, 1987, the day after so-called "Black Monday".
The Toronto exchange was forced to close 30 minutes early after experiencing system problems soon after Bre-X shares resumed trading.
On Nasdaq, Bre-X's stock plummeted to $1.97 in heavy turnover of 6.8 million shares on Thursday after closing at $11.375 on Tuesday. The stock was also halted on Nasdaq on Wednesday.
Walsh has made millions of dollars from the discovery and now lives in luxury in the Bahamas.
Earlier this week, he complained about rumours that the find might be overstated and even threatened legal action "against certain parties and publications."

However, Walsh admitted Wednesday "there appears to be a strong possibility that the potential gold resources on the Busang project in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, have been overstated because of invalid samples and assaying of those samples."
New Orleans-based Freeport McMoRan set off alarm bells on Wednesday by saying its own assays "indicate insignificant amounts of gold."
Freeport's stock closed up 50 cents at $30.125 on Thursday after sinking sharply on the New York Stock Exchange on the previous day.
Bre-X earlier this year issued confirmed estimates that the Busang deposit held at least 71 million ounces of gold, worth about $20 billion at current gold prices.
At that level, Busang would be the biggest gold find since the discovery of the Witwatersrand goldfields in South Africa in the late 1800s.

Bre-X's head of exploration, John Felderhof, said last month he was "comfortable" with estimates that Busang might contain up to 200 million ounces of gold. Walsh said Felderhof stood by the company's reserve estimates after visiting Busang this week.
Bre-X shares sank last week after an Indonesian newspaper report quoted unnamed sources as saying Freeport, which holds 15 percent of Busang, had doubts about the size and viability of the deposit.
The rumours were fanned to fever pitch by the death, billed as a suicide, of Bre-X chief geologist Michael de Guzman, who fell from a helicopter en route to Busang last week.

Bre-X and Walsh had been the envy of the international mining community since Walsh gambled the company's last C$10,000 ($7,280) in 1993 and claimed to have struck a mother lode of gold in Indonesia's East Kalimantan province.
